source.title: The Science of Getting Rich
source.attribution: Wallace D. Wattles, The Science of Getting Rich, Project Gutenberg, public domain
source.notes: Cards use only the book's practical advice (gratitude, focused daily effort, giving value). Its claims that thought alone creates wealth are not presented.

cards.title: Gratitude keeps you from sliding into constant dissatisfaction
cards.body:
Wattles saw gratitude as a guard against a habit that quietly drains people: dwelling on everything that is wrong, lacking or unfair. A mind fixed on complaints starts to see little else, and that makes it harder to spot opportunities or act well.

Gratitude does not mean ignoring problems. It means noticing what is working, who has helped you and what you already have, so that you approach your goals from steadiness rather than resentment. A short daily habit of naming a few good things is enough to shift the tone of a day.
cards.quote: Without gratitude you cannot long keep from dissatisfied thought regarding things as they are.
cards.locator: Chapter VII. Gratitude ¶16
cards.apply_it: Tonight, write down three specific things that went well today and who or what helped make them happen.

quiz.question: What did Wattles say gratitude protects you from?
options: Settling into dissatisfied thought about how things are
quiz.explanation: Without gratitude, he argued, the mind drifts into dwelling on what is wrong and lacking.

cards.title: To move up, first more than fill your current role
cards.body:
Wattles argued that you advance by becoming bigger than your present position, and you cannot be bigger than a job you are only half doing. People who leave parts of their current work undone rarely get trusted with more.

For a raise or promotion, this is practical advice. Do every part of your present role well, then go a little beyond it: solve a problem nobody assigned, help a teammate, improve a process. That surplus is what managers and clients notice when they choose who gets more responsibility and pay.
cards.quote: You can advance only by being larger than your present place; and no man is larger than his present place who leaves undone any of the work pertaining to that place.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Efficient Action ¶2
cards.apply_it: List the parts of your job you tend to neglect. Finish one of them this week, then add one small piece of value nobody asked for.

quiz.question: According to Wattles, who is not 'larger than his present place'?
options: Someone who asks for a raise
Someone who leaves undone any of the work of that place
quiz.explanation: You cannot outgrow a role while parts of it are still undone.

cards.title: Do each day's work fully, and only that day's
cards.body:
Wattles treated each day as either a success or a failure on its own terms. If something could be done today and you skip it, that small gap can matter more than you expect. So he urged doing everything that can be done each day.

He added an important limit: this is not a call to overwork, rush, or cram a week's work into one day. The point is steady, complete days rather than heroic sprints. A finished, sustainable day repeated many times beats bursts of effort followed by collapse.
cards.quote: Do, every day, all that you can do that day, and do each act in an efficient manner.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Efficient Action ¶29
cards.apply_it: Write down what a complete, realistic day looks like for you tomorrow, then stop when it is done instead of piling on more.

quiz.question: What limit did Wattles put on doing everything you can each day?
options: Do not overwork or try to do tomorrow's work today
quiz.explanation: He warned against rushing or doing a week's work in a day; the aim is full, efficient days.

cards.title: Count the actions that work, not the busy ones
cards.body:
Wattles pointed out that doing many things badly gets you nowhere. Each act is either effective or not, and a pile of half-hearted, scattered actions adds up to failure no matter how busy it feels.

Modern work makes this easy to forget: dozens of messages, meetings and tabs can fill a day while little moves forward. Doing fewer things, and giving each your full attention so it actually lands, usually produces more than frantic multitasking. Judge your day by what it achieved, not by how full it was.
cards.quote: The cause of failure is doing too many things in an inefficient manner, and not doing enough things in an efficient manner.
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Efficient Action ¶20
cards.apply_it: At the end of today, list what you finished well rather than everything you touched. What would you drop tomorrow to make that list longer?

quiz.question: What did Wattles name as the cause of failure?
options: Doing too many things inefficiently and too few efficiently
quiz.explanation: It is the quality of each action, not the sheer number, that decides the result.

cards.title: Give people more value than the price you charge
cards.body:
Wattles separated cash value, what someone pays, from use value, what they actually get out of it. A book may cost little in paper and ink, but if its ideas help the reader earn far more, the reader was not short-changed.

His rule was to make every deal give the other person more use value than the cash you take. For a freelancer, shop or employee, that means aiming for customers who feel they got a bargain. It is fair, and it is also what brings people back and makes them recommend you.
cards.quote: Give every man more in use value than you take from him in cash value; then you are adding to the life of the world by every business transaction.
cards.locator: Chapter VI. How Riches Come to You ¶6
cards.apply_it: Pick one product, service or task you deliver. What small addition would make the person receiving it feel they got more than they paid for?

quiz.question: What did Wattles mean by giving more 'use value' than 'cash value'?
options: Making sure people get more benefit than the money they pay
quiz.explanation: Use value is the benefit received; he wanted it to exceed the cash paid in every transaction.

cards.title: Be clear about what your money is actually for
cards.body:
Wattles grounded his case for earning more in ordinary needs. To live fully in body, he wrote, people need good food, decent clothes, warm shelter, rest and freedom from crushing overwork. To grow in mind they need books and time to read them, chances to travel and observe, and good company to think with. And love, he said, needs the means to give.

That list is a useful test for your own goals. Money that buys rest, learning and the ability to care for people you love is doing real work. Money chased for its own sake rarely satisfies.
cards.quote: He cannot live fully in mind without books and time to study them, without opportunity for travel and observation, or without intellectual companionship.
cards.locator: Chapter I. The Right to Be Rich ¶11
cards.apply_it: Write down three things you want more money for. Do they serve your body, your mind or the people you love?

quiz.question: Which of these did Wattles list as a need for living fully in mind?
options: Books and time to study them
quiz.explanation: He wrote that a person cannot live fully in mind without books and time to study them, travel and good company.

cards.title: Love naturally shows itself in giving
cards.body:
Wattles believed people find their greatest happiness in doing good for those they love, and that love expresses itself most naturally through giving. Part of his argument for earning well was simply that it lets you provide for family, help friends and contribute to your community.

Giving isn't only money: time, attention, skills and care count too. But it's worth noticing how much quiet satisfaction comes from being able to give generously. Building your means is, in part, building your capacity to love in practical ways.
cards.quote: Man's highest happiness is found in the bestowal of benefits on those he loves; love finds its most natural and spontaneous expression in giving.
cards.locator: Chapter I. The Right to Be Rich ¶14
cards.apply_it: Do one practical kindness this week for someone you love: a meal, a repair, a school fee, or an afternoon of your time.

quiz.question: According to Wattles, where does love find its most natural expression?
quiz.explanation: He wrote that love finds its most natural and spontaneous expression in giving.

cards.title: Wanting a fuller, better-resourced life is nothing to be ashamed of
cards.body:
Many people feel guilty about wanting more money, as if ambition were greedy. Wattles disagreed: the desire for wealth, he said, is really the desire for a richer, fuller life, and that is praiseworthy. He wanted readers to stop apologising for hoping to live well.

He pushed this further than many would, even calling contentment with little a fault. A balanced reading keeps the useful core: honest ambition for a better life for yourself and your family is healthy, provided you pursue it fairly and remember what the money is for.
cards.quote: There is nothing wrong in wanting to get rich. The desire for riches is really the desire for a richer, fuller, and more abundant life; and that desire is praiseworthy.
cards.locator: Chapter I. The Right to Be Rich ¶7
cards.apply_it: Write one sentence describing the fuller life you want. Notice whether any guilt shows up, and ask if it's really justified.

quiz.question: How did Wattles describe the desire for riches?
options: As the desire for a richer, fuller life
quiz.explanation: He called it 'really the desire for a richer, fuller, and more abundant life', which he considered praiseworthy.

cards.title: If someone in your trade and town is thriving, study what they do
cards.body:
Wattles noticed that rich and poor often live on the same street and work in the same trades. When two people run the same kind of business in the same place and one prospers while the other struggles, he argued, the difference lies largely in how they do things.

Circumstances still matter, and some start with far more help. But the comparison points you to something you can act on. Watch the people in your line who are doing well: how they treat customers, price, follow up and manage money. Then adapt what you learn.
cards.quote: When two men are in the same locality, and in the same business, and one gets rich while the other remains poor, it shows that getting rich is not, primarily, a matter of environment.
cards.locator: Chapter II. There Is a Science of Getting Rich ¶6
cards.apply_it: Identify one person in your field and area who is doing well. List three things they do differently from you.

quiz.question: What did Wattles conclude from two people in the same business and place getting different results?
options: The difference lies largely in how they do things
quiz.explanation: He argued it shows success is not primarily environment but the way things are done.

cards.title: Talent is a tool; what counts is how well you use it
cards.body:
Wattles observed that plenty of gifted musicians, skilled craftsmen and able traders stay poor. Talents, he said, are like tools: you need good ones, but a sharp saw and plane in one carpenter's hands make fine furniture, while the same tools in another's produce a botch.

It's a useful corrective to waiting until you feel talented enough. Skill matters, but so do habits, judgement and consistency in applying it. Focus on how you use what you have: the quality of your work, how you deal with people, and how steadily you improve.
cards.quote: The different faculties are tools; it is essential to have good tools, but it is also essential that the tools should be used in the Right Way.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. Getting Into the Right Business ¶3
cards.apply_it: Pick one skill you already have. What is one way you could use it more effectively this week?

quiz.question: How did Wattles illustrate the difference between having talent and using it well?
options: Two carpenters with the same tools producing different results
quiz.explanation: He described one man making handsome furniture and another making a botch with the same good tools.

cards.title: Set up where your customers actually are
cards.body:
Although Wattles played down circumstances, he admitted location counts. You wouldn't open a business in the middle of the Sahara, he joked; an ice-cream parlour does better in a warm climate than in Greenland, and a salmon fishery needs salmon. Business means dealing with people, so you need to be where people who want what you offer can reach you.

Today that may mean a busy street, a market day, or the right online platform. Before investing, check that the people you hope to serve are actually there.
cards.quote: Getting rich involves the necessity of dealing with men, and of being where there are people to deal with
cards.locator: Chapter II. There Is a Science of Getting Rich ¶16
cards.apply_it: For your product or service, name where your customers spend time, in person or online. Are you there?

quiz.question: Which example did Wattles use to show that location matters?
options: An ice-cream parlour doing better in a warm climate than in Greenland
quiz.explanation: He noted an ice-cream parlour would do better in a warm climate than in Greenland.

cards.title: Start improving from exactly where you are now
cards.body:
Wattles insisted that lacking capital, connections or the right job doesn't stop you starting. If you have no capital, you can build it; if you're in the wrong work or the wrong place, you can move. But the route there begins in your present job and location, by working better where you stand.

It's a practical answer to the trap of 'once I have X, I'll start'. Waiting for perfect conditions usually means waiting forever. Small improvements in your current situation build the savings, skills and reputation that make the next move possible.
cards.quote: If you have no capital, you can get capital; if you are in the wrong business, you can get into the right business; if you are in the wrong location, you can go to the right location
cards.locator: Chapter II. There Is a Science of Getting Rich ¶23
cards.apply_it: Finish this sentence: 'Once I have ___, I'll start.' Then list one step you can take toward your goal without it.

quiz.question: Where did Wattles say the path to a better position begins?
options: Once you move to a big city
In your present business and present location
quiz.explanation: He said you get to the right business and place by beginning in your present business and location.

cards.title: Look for growing fields, not ones already dominated
cards.body:
Writing in 1910, Wattles told readers not to fight the railroad giants for a share of a monopolised industry. Electric railways were still young, he said, and air transport would soon employ huge numbers; why not turn your attention there? He was right about flight.

The advice still applies. Competing head-on with established giants is hard. New and growing fields have fewer gatekeepers and more room for newcomers. Keep an eye on what's emerging in your area, from new services to new technologies, and ask where demand is rising fastest.
cards.quote: Probably it would be hard for you to get control of any of the great railroad systems; that field is pretty well monopolized. But the electric railway business is still in its infancy, and offers plenty of scope for enterprise
cards.locator: Chapter III. Is Opportunity Monopolized? ¶1
cards.apply_it: List three services or products in your area where demand seems to be growing faster than the number of people supplying them.

quiz.question: What did Wattles suggest instead of competing in the monopolised steam railway business?
options: Turning to young, growing fields like electric railways and air transport
quiz.explanation: He pointed to electric railways and future air transport as fields with plenty of scope for enterprise.

cards.title: Sustained, careful thinking is hard work most people avoid
cards.body:
Wattles observed that there's no labour people shrink from more than sustained, consecutive thought; he called it the hardest work in the world. It's easy to react to whatever is in front of you and much harder to think a problem through, especially when the evidence around you seems to point the other way.

That makes deliberate thinking a quiet advantage. Setting aside time to work through a decision step by step, on paper, without distractions, is something few people do. Those who do it tend to make better choices.
cards.quote: There is no labor from which most people shrink as they do from that of sustained and consecutive thought; it is the hardest work in the world.
cards.locator: Chapter IV. The First Principle in the Science of Getting Rich ¶23
cards.apply_it: Take one decision you've been avoiding. Spend 30 uninterrupted minutes writing out the options and their likely results.

quiz.question: What did Wattles call 'the hardest work in the world'?
quiz.explanation: He wrote that people shrink most from sustained and consecutive thought, the hardest work in the world.

cards.title: Making the most of yourself is how you help others most
cards.body:
Wattles rejected the idea that the noblest life is total self-sacrifice. Extreme altruism, he wrote, is no better than extreme selfishness; both are mistakes. A full life includes the body's needs, the mind's growth and care for others, without neglecting any of them.

His practical point: you can usually help others more by developing yourself than by running yourself down. A rested, skilled, financially stable person has far more to give than one who is exhausted and broke. Looking after your own growth isn't selfish; it is what makes lasting generosity possible.
cards.quote: But remember that extreme altruism is no better and no nobler than extreme selfishness; both are mistakes.
cards.locator: Chapter V. Increasing Life ¶20
cards.apply_it: Are you neglecting your own rest, health or growth in order to serve others? Choose one way to invest in yourself this week.

quiz.question: What did Wattles say about extreme altruism?
options: It is the noblest way to live
It is no better than extreme selfishness
quiz.explanation: He wrote that extreme altruism is no better and no nobler than extreme selfishness; both are mistakes.

cards.title: Build wealth by creating value, not by squeezing people
cards.body:
Wattles urged readers to be creators rather than competitors. You don't need to cheat, drive sharp bargains, take advantage of anyone, or pay workers less than they earn. Wealth made by creating something useful leaves others better off, while wealth grabbed from others keeps people down behind you.

This isn't naive about business: you still negotiate and make a profit. But it sets a firm line. If your income depends on underpaying, misleading or exploiting people, it's built on weak ground. Fair pay and honest dealing are part of building something that lasts.
cards.quote: You do not have to cheat, or to take advantage. You do not need to let any man work for you for less than he earns.
cards.locator: Chapter V. Increasing Life ¶29
cards.apply_it: Review how you pay or deal with the people who work with you. Is anyone getting less than their work is worth?

quiz.question: According to Wattles, what does a 'creator' not need to do?
options: Cheat, take advantage, or underpay workers
quiz.explanation: He wrote that you do not have to cheat, take advantage, or let anyone work for you for less than he earns.

cards.title: Run your business as a ladder your people can climb
cards.body:
Wattles accepted that employers must earn more from workers than they pay them; otherwise there's no business. But he urged owners to organise things so every employee who wants to advance can do so a little every day: learning skills, taking on responsibility and moving up. The business becomes a ladder, not a trap.

For small business owners and managers, this means training people, promoting from within and sharing knowledge. Staff who see a path upward work with more energy, and the business grows with them.
cards.quote: You can so conduct your business that it will be a sort of ladder, by which every employee who will take the trouble may climb to riches himself
cards.locator: Chapter VI. How Riches Come to You ¶8
cards.apply_it: If you manage anyone, ask each person what skill they'd like to learn next, and find one way to help them learn it.

quiz.question: What image did Wattles use for a business that helps employees advance?
quiz.explanation: He said a business can be conducted as 'a sort of ladder' by which employees may climb.

cards.title: Vague wishes go nowhere; get specific about what you want
cards.body:
Wattles noted that almost everyone has a general wish for more money, travel or a better life, and that such vague longings achieve little. He compared it to sending a telegram: you wouldn't send the alphabet and let your friend build the message; you'd send a clear sentence.

Set aside his metaphysics and the practical point stands. A specific goal, such as a particular savings figure by a particular date or a defined skill or role, tells you what to do next and lets you measure progress. 'I want to be better off' doesn't.
cards.quote: you must know what you want, and be definite.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Thinking in the Certain Way ¶4
cards.apply_it: Rewrite one vague goal as a specific one: what exactly, how much, and by when?

quiz.question: What comparison did Wattles use to show why goals must be definite?
options: Sending a message as random letters instead of a clear sentence
quiz.explanation: He said you wouldn't send the alphabet in order and let a friend construct the message; you'd send a coherent sentence.

cards.title: A clear picture of your goal is useless without the purpose to act
cards.body:
Wattles told readers to picture what they wanted in detail, but warned that this alone makes you a dreamer with little power to accomplish anything. Behind the vision there must be a firm purpose to bring it about in real, tangible form.

Vision boards and daydreams can be motivating, but they can also feel like progress while nothing changes. The useful part of imagining a goal is that it guides action: it tells you what to work on today. If the picture isn't changing what you do, it's entertainment, not a plan.
cards.quote: If that is all you do, you are only a dreamer, and will have little or no power for accomplishment.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Thinking in the Certain Way ¶13
cards.apply_it: Take a goal you often imagine. Write the very next physical action that moves it forward, and do it today.

quiz.question: What did Wattles say someone becomes if they only picture their goal clearly?
options: A dreamer with little power to accomplish
quiz.explanation: He said that if seeing the picture is all you do, you are only a dreamer with little power for accomplishment.

cards.title: If staying focused on a goal takes huge effort, check how much you want it
cards.body:
Wattles made a sharp observation about attention: you don't need concentration exercises to think about something you truly want. It's the things you don't really care about that take effort to keep in mind. A goal that genuinely matters to you tends to stay in your thoughts by itself.

So if you constantly have to force yourself to remember a goal, it's worth asking whether it's really yours, or one you feel you should want. Sometimes the fix is a better reason; sometimes it's a different goal.
cards.quote: it is the things you do not really care about which require effort to fix your attention upon them.
cards.locator: Chapter VIII. Thinking in the Certain Way ¶9
cards.apply_it: For a goal you keep forgetting, write down why it matters to you personally. If you can't, consider whether to drop or change it.

quiz.question: According to Wattles, which things require effort to keep your attention on?
options: Things you do not really care about
quiz.explanation: He wrote that it is the things you do not really care about which require effort to fix your attention on them.

cards.title: Don't try to force your will on other people, even for their own good
cards.body:
Wattles was firm that pressuring people to do what you want is wrong, whether by physical force or psychological pressure. Coercing someone mentally, he said, is as much a violation as coercing them physically. He extended it even to 'helping': you have no right to impose your will on someone for their own good, because you don't truly know what their good is.

That's a healthy rule in families, workplaces and friendships. Offer information, ask, persuade honestly, and then respect the other person's right to choose.
cards.quote: You have no right to use your will power upon another person, even ‘for his own good’; for you do not know what is for his good.
cards.locator: Chapter IX. How to Use the Will ¶5
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you're trying to push into a decision. Share your view once, clearly, then leave the choice to them.

quiz.question: Why did Wattles say you shouldn't impose your will on others even 'for their own good'?
options: You do not know what is truly for their good
quiz.explanation: He wrote that you have no right to use your will on another person, 'for you do not know what is for his good'.

cards.title: Point your willpower at yourself, not at other people
cards.body:
Having ruled out pushing others around, Wattles said the right place for willpower is yourself. Once you know what to think and do, use your will to hold yourself to it: to keep working, to stay on course, to direct your attention where it should go.

This cuts down a lot of wasted energy. Much frustration comes from trying to control people and events we can't. Redirecting that effort into our own habits, choices and focus is both more respectful and far more effective.
cards.quote: That is the legitimate use of the will in getting what you want--to use it in holding yourself to the right course.
cards.locator: Chapter IX. How to Use the Will ¶13
cards.apply_it: Notice one situation where you're trying to change someone else. What could you change in your own actions instead?

quiz.question: What did Wattles call the legitimate use of willpower?
options: Holding yourself to the right course
quiz.explanation: He said the legitimate use of the will is holding yourself to the right course.

cards.title: You can only act where you are, so act there
cards.body:
Wattles pointed out something obvious that's easy to forget: you can't act in the past, you can't act in the future, and you can't act somewhere you aren't. The only place you can do anything is here, now, with the people and things around you.

That cuts through a lot of mental clutter. Regret about what you should have done and plans about what you'll do someday both feel productive but change nothing. The question that matters is: what can I do from here, today?
cards.quote: You cannot act where you are not; you cannot act where you have been, and you cannot act where you are going to be; you can act only where you are.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. Acting in the Certain Way ¶21
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself: given exactly where I am today, what's one step toward my goal I can take in the next hour?

quiz.question: According to Wattles, where can you take action?
options: Where you are going to be
quiz.explanation: He wrote that you can act only where you are, not where you have been or where you will be.

cards.title: Give the task in front of you your whole mind
cards.body:
Wattles warned that doing one thing while your thoughts are busy with tomorrow splits your attention and weakens the work. His instruction was simple: bring all of your attention to what you are doing now.

It's an early description of what we now call being present. Half-attending to a conversation while planning the next meeting, or working while worrying about next month, produces weaker work and more stress. Whatever you're doing, do that one thing with full attention, then move to the next.
cards.quote: If you act in the present with your mind on the future, your present action will be with a divided mind, and will not be effective.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. Acting in the Certain Way ¶17
cards.apply_it: For your next task, put your phone away and close other tabs. Give it your full attention for 25 minutes.

quiz.question: What did Wattles say happens when you act with your mind on the future?
options: Your action is done with a divided mind and is less effective
quiz.explanation: He said action taken with your mind on the future is done with a divided mind and will not be effective.

cards.title: Use the job you have as the route to the job you want
cards.body:
Wattles told readers who felt stuck in the wrong work not to wait for the right job before starting to act. Don't wait for a better environment to come to you, he said; get to it by acting well in the one you're in, treating today's position as the vehicle for reaching a better one.

In practice: build skills on the job that the next role needs, earn references by doing excellent work, save money that gives you freedom to move, and make contacts. The current job becomes a stepping stone instead of a waiting room.
cards.quote: Use your present business as the means of getting a better one, and use your present environment as the means of getting into a better one.
cards.locator: Chapter XI. Acting in the Certain Way ¶32
cards.apply_it: List two skills or contacts your dream job needs. How could your current job help you build one of them this month?

quiz.question: What did Wattles advise people who feel they're in the wrong business?
options: Use their present business as the means of getting a better one
quiz.explanation: He said not to wait, but to use the present business and environment as the means of getting into a better one.

cards.title: Don't spend today rehearsing every possible future disaster
cards.body:
Wattles advised against using today's energy to plan for every emergency that might someday arise, unless it changes what you should do today. Deal with obstacles when they actually come close, he said; many shrink or show a way around as you approach.

He overstated it: some preparation, like an emergency fund or insurance, is plainly sensible. But endless 'what if' thinking drains energy, feeds worry, and rarely produces better plans. Prepare reasonably, then bring your attention back to the work in front of you.
cards.quote: Do not spend any time in planning as to how you will meet possible emergencies in the future, except as the necessary policies may affect your actions to-day.
cards.locator: Chapter XVI. Some Cautions, and Concluding Observations ¶12
cards.apply_it: Write down a future worry. If there's a sensible step to take today, take it. Otherwise, set the worry aside until it's actually near.

quiz.question: When did Wattles think it was worth planning for possible future emergencies?
options: Only when it affects what you should do today
quiz.explanation: He advised against such planning except as it affects your actions today.

cards.title: An ounce of doing is worth a pound of theorising
cards.body:
Wattles described people who are poor not from lack of effort or knowledge, but because they're lost among competing theories and systems, trying a little of each and failing at all. His remedy was to pick a way and practise it, since a small amount of doing is worth far more than a great deal of theorising.

It applies to fitness plans, business courses and productivity methods alike. Reading about ten approaches feels like progress. Choosing one reasonable approach and actually doing it for a few months teaches you more than any amount of comparison.
cards.quote: an ounce of doing things is worth a pound of theorizing.
cards.locator: Chapter X. Further Use of the Will ¶27
cards.apply_it: Which area of your life are you researching instead of acting on? Pick one method and commit to it for 30 days.

quiz.question: What problem did Wattles see in people lost among many theories and systems?
options: They try a mixture of many systems and fail in all
quiz.explanation: He said they try a mixture of many systems and fail in all; an ounce of doing is worth a pound of theorising.

cards.title: You can build abilities you weren't born with
cards.body:
Wattles said you'll find success easiest in work that suits the talents you already have well developed. But he refused to treat your starting abilities as fixed. If a line of work needs a talent you lack, you can develop it; you'll just have to make your tools as you go, rather than relying only on those you were born with.

It may be harder and slower, but most skills, from public speaking to accounting to design, can be learned with practice. Don't rule out a path just because it doesn't come naturally yet.
cards.quote: it merely means that you will have to make your tools as you go along, instead of confining yourself to the use of those with which you were born.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. Getting Into the Right Business ¶6
cards.apply_it: Name one skill you've told yourself 'I'm just not good at'. Find one beginner resource and practise it for 15 minutes.

quiz.question: What did Wattles say about pursuing work for which you lack natural talent?
options: You can develop the talent, making your tools as you go
quiz.explanation: He said you can develop the needed talent; you just have to make your tools as you go along.

cards.title: If you must do work you dislike, treat it as the road to work you want
cards.body:
Wattles believed you'll be most satisfied doing work you actually want to do, and that it's legitimate to aim for it. But he was realistic: past choices or circumstances may leave you doing work you dislike for a while.

His suggestion was to change how you see it: when the current job is clearly a means to reach the work you want, it becomes more bearable, even pleasant. That only works if it really is a means, so make sure the job is building money, skills or contacts that move you toward the goal.
cards.quote: you can make the doing of it pleasant by knowing that it is making it possible for you to come to the doing of what you want to do.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. Getting Into the Right Business ¶15
cards.apply_it: Write down how your current job is helping you reach the work you want. If it isn't, what would need to change?

quiz.question: How did Wattles suggest making disliked work more bearable?
options: By seeing it as the means to reach the work you want
quiz.explanation: He said you can make it pleasant by knowing it is making it possible to reach the work you want.

cards.title: Change direction by steady growth, and don't leap while in doubt
cards.body:
For people who feel they're in the wrong line of work, Wattles counselled patience. Don't rush into another field, he said; the best way to change your work or surroundings is usually gradual growth. He wasn't against bold moves: if a real opportunity appears and, after careful thought, you're convinced it's right, take it. But never make sudden, radical changes while you're still unsure.

It's sound advice for resignations, relocations and big investments. Doubt is a signal to gather more information, test on a small scale, or wait.
cards.quote: never take sudden or radical action when you are in doubt as to the wisdom of doing so.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. Getting Into the Right Business ¶17
cards.apply_it: If you're considering a big change, list what would make you confident. Find one small, low-risk way to test it first.

quiz.question: What did Wattles advise about making radical changes?
options: Never make them while you are in doubt
Make them only when others agree
quiz.explanation: He said not to fear a sudden change when it's clearly right, but never to take radical action while in doubt.

cards.title: Go as fast as you can, but never hurry
cards.body:
Wattles drew a fine distinction between speed and hurry. Do everything you can each day, he said, and do it well, but without haste, worry or fear. Moving quickly with a steady mind is productive; rushing in a panic leads to mistakes and a sense of scarcity. When you catch yourself hurrying, he advised, stop and refocus on what you're aiming for.

Hurry often signals that anxiety is driving, not judgement. Working briskly but calmly tends to produce better results and leaves you less drained at the end of the day.
cards.quote: Do all that you can do in a perfect manner every day, but do it without haste, worry, or fear. Go as fast as you can, but never hurry.
cards.locator: Chapter XIII. Getting Into the Right Business ¶24
cards.apply_it: When you notice yourself rushing today, pause for a breath, name the single next step, and continue at a steady pace.

quiz.question: How did Wattles distinguish speed from hurry?
options: Hurry is better for small tasks
Go as fast as you can, but without haste, worry or fear
quiz.explanation: He advised doing all you can each day without haste, worry or fear: 'Go as fast as you can, but never hurry.'

cards.title: Make sure people leave every dealing with you better off
cards.body:
Wattles said people are drawn to anyone who helps them get ahead. So in every transaction, even selling a sweet to a child, aim for the other person to feel they have gained by dealing with you. Give them more real usefulness than the money you take, and let your manner show that you want them to advance too.

It's a good test for a seller, employee or colleague: do people come away from contact with you better informed, better served or more encouraged? Those who do tend to come back, and to bring others.
cards.quote: You must so impress others that they will feel that in associating with you they will get increase for themselves.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV. The Impression of Increase ¶19
cards.apply_it: After your next three customer or colleague interactions, ask: did this person leave better off than they came?

quiz.question: What did Wattles want every customer or contact to feel?
options: That associating with you helps them get ahead
quiz.explanation: He said others should feel that in associating with you they will get increase for themselves.

cards.title: Real confidence is quiet; boasting usually hides doubt
cards.body:
Wattles told readers not to brag about their success or talk about it more than necessary. In his view, bragging is usually a sign of hidden insecurity: people who boast are often privately unsure and anxious. Genuine confidence shows in steady action and a calm manner, and doesn't need words to announce it.

That matches what many people notice at work and online: the loudest claims often come from the least secure. Let results and reliability speak; people will sense quiet assurance without being told.
cards.quote: Wherever you find a boastful person, you find one who is secretly doubtful and afraid.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV. The Impression of Increase ¶18
cards.apply_it: Before you next share an achievement, ask whether you're informing people or trying to convince yourself.

quiz.question: What did Wattles believe boastfulness usually reveals?
quiz.explanation: He wrote that wherever you find a boastful person, you find one who is secretly doubtful and afraid.

cards.title: Beware the urge to rule over others or impress with display
cards.body:
Wattles warned of an 'insidious temptation': the desire for power over other people. He blamed it for wars between kings and for ruthless business empires. In everyday life, he said, it shows up as wanting authority, wanting to be seen as above ordinary people, and trying to impress others with lavish display.

You don't need to dominate anyone to shape your own life. Chasing status and control pulls you into endless comparison and conflict. Building something useful, and wanting others to rise too, is a steadier path.
cards.quote: Look out for the temptation to seek for authority, to become a ‘master,’ to be considered as one who is above the common herd, to impress others by lavish display, and so on.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV. The Impression of Increase ¶27
cards.apply_it: Notice one purchase or habit that's mainly about being seen as above others. What would you choose if no one could see?

quiz.question: Which of these did Wattles list as a form of the temptation to seek power?
quiz.explanation: He warned against seeking authority, being seen as above the 'common herd', and impressing others by lavish display.

cards.title: Want for everyone what you want for yourself
cards.body:
Wattles closed his warning about power with a line from Samuel 'Golden Rule' Jones, the reforming mayor of Toledo, Ohio, whose motto was to wish for everyone the same good things he wished for himself. Wattles thought no better statement of the right spirit could be written.

It's a simple check on ambition. If you want security, fair pay, respect and opportunity for yourself, ask whether your choices also support those things for the people around you: staff, customers, neighbours, family. Success that others can share tends to be more secure and more satisfying.
cards.quote: What I want for myself, I want for everybody.
cards.locator: Chapter XIV. The Impression of Increase ¶29
cards.apply_it: Write down one thing you want for yourself this year. Name one person you could help get the same.

quiz.question: Whose motto did Wattles quote as the best statement of creative, non-competitive action?
quiz.explanation: He quoted 'Golden Rule' Jones of Toledo: 'What I want for myself, I want for everybody.'

cards.title: Good work alone may keep you in place; know where you're heading
cards.body:
Wattles made an uncomfortable point: a worker who simply does an excellent job and is satisfied with that is valuable to the employer, which is exactly why the employer may not promote them. They're worth more where they are.

His advice was to do excellent work for your own growth rather than just to please the boss, and to have a clear idea of what you want to become. That means building skills for the next role, letting people know your ambitions, and being ready to move elsewhere if no path opens where you are.
cards.quote: The man who is merely a ‘good’ workman, filling his place to the very best of his ability, and satisfied with that, is valuable to his employer; and it is not to the employer's interest to promote him
cards.locator: Chapter XV. The Advancing Man ¶12
cards.apply_it: Tell your manager or a mentor what role you'd like next, and ask what skills you'd need to show for it.

quiz.question: Why might an employer not promote a merely 'good' worker, according to Wattles?
options: Good workers are easy to replace
Such a worker is worth more to the employer where he is
quiz.explanation: He said a good worker satisfied with his place is valuable there, so it is not in the employer's interest to promote him.

cards.title: Don't wait for the perfect opportunity; take the next step up
cards.body:
Wattles told readers not to hold out for an opportunity to become everything they want to be in one move. When a chance comes to be more than you are now, and you feel drawn to it, take it. It will be the first step toward something greater.

Careers and businesses rarely jump straight to the goal. A slightly bigger role, a new skill, a small contract or a modest promotion often leads to the next. Turning down good steps while waiting for the ideal one can leave you exactly where you started.
cards.quote: when an opportunity to be more than you are now is presented and you feel impelled toward it, take it. It will be the first step toward a greater opportunity.
cards.locator: Chapter XV. The Advancing Man ¶22
cards.apply_it: Is there an offer or opening you've dismissed because it isn't 'the big one'? Reconsider whether it's a good next step.

quiz.question: What did Wattles advise when a chance comes to be more than you are now?
options: Take it as a first step toward greater opportunity
Only accept if it doubles your pay
quiz.explanation: He said to take it, because it will be the first step toward a greater opportunity.

cards.title: Watch how you talk about yourself and your situation
cards.body:
Wattles advised readers to guard their speech and never talk about themselves or their affairs in a discouraged or discouraging way. Constant complaint, he believed, reinforces a defeated mindset in you and in those listening.

He pushed it to extremes, like never admitting failure is possible, which isn't wise; problems need honest discussion with people who can help. But the core holds up: the stories you repeat about yourself, such as 'I'm always broke' or 'nothing works for me', shape what you expect and try. Speak about difficulties accurately, without turning them into your identity.
cards.quote: Guard your speech. Never speak of yourself, your affairs, or of anything else in a discouraged or discouraging way.
cards.locator: Chapter XVI. Some Cautions, and Concluding Observations ¶17
cards.apply_it: Catch one discouraging phrase you often say about yourself. Replace it with an accurate, constructive version.

quiz.question: What did Wattles advise about the way you speak of yourself and your affairs?
options: Never in a discouraged or discouraging way
quiz.explanation: He wrote: 'Guard your speech. Never speak of yourself, your affairs, or of anything else in a discouraged or discouraging way.'

cards.title: A deal that falls through can clear the way for a better one
cards.body:
Wattles told of a student who worked for weeks on a business deal that seemed ideal, only to see it collapse at the last moment. Instead of sinking into disappointment, he carried on steadily. A few weeks later a far better opportunity arrived, one he could not have taken had the first deal gone through.

Not every setback hides a better outcome. But treating a lost opportunity as the end of the story can stop you noticing the next one. Grieve briefly, learn what you can, and keep moving.
cards.quote: In a few weeks an opportunity so much better came his way that he would not have made the first deal on any account
cards.locator: Chapter XVI. Some Cautions, and Concluding Observations ¶25
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent disappointment. Write down one door it might leave open that wasn't open before.

quiz.question: What happened to the student after his business deal collapsed?
options: He tried the same deal again
A much better opportunity came a few weeks later
quiz.explanation: He kept going without disappointment, and soon a far better opportunity came that he would not have traded for the first deal.

cards.title: Each success makes the next one easier
cards.body:
Wattles noted that successful action is cumulative: each well-done act opens the way to further successes, so progress speeds up over time. People and opportunities are drawn to someone who is visibly moving forward.

This is a good argument for starting with achievable wins. Finishing one small project well builds skill, confidence, reputation and contacts, all of which make the next project easier. Slow early progress isn't a sign of failure; it's the stage before momentum builds.
cards.quote: every success opens the way to other successes
cards.locator: Chapter XII. Efficient Action ¶27
cards.apply_it: Choose one small task you can complete well today. Finish it fully, then note what it makes easier tomorrow.

quiz.question: What did Wattles say about the results of successful action?
options: They are cumulative, each success opening the way to others
quiz.explanation: He wrote that successful action is cumulative in its results and every success opens the way to other successes.
